# Glossary {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begingroup\small
```

One plain sentence for each term, and the chapter where it's explained fully.

Act, review, escalate
: The three zones of a decision policy: handle it automatically, send it to a person, or raise it urgently (Chapter 10).

Agent
: A program that uses a model to observe, decide and act in a loop, calling tools along the way (Chapter 5).

Attention
: A way for each word in a sequence to look at the others and decide which ones matter for its meaning (Chapter 4).

Audit (random)
: Sending a random share of automatically handled cases to a person, so that mistakes the system is sure about still get seen (Chapter 10).

AUC
: The chance that a model gives a randomly chosen real case a higher score than a randomly chosen harmless one. It measures ranking, not calibration (Chapter 2).

Base rate
: How common something is before you look at any evidence, like the share of alerts that are real threats (Chapter 2).


Calibration
: A model is calibrated when the things it calls 70% likely happen about 70% of the time: its probabilities are honest (Chapter 2).

Capacity
: How many cases the people in the loop can handle in a day. A policy that ignores it isn't a policy (Chapter 10).


CISO
: Chief information security officer: the person in charge of an organisation's security (Chapter 6).

Choice
: A typed question with a set of named options. The answer is a probability for each option, adding up to 1 (Chapter 7).

Confidence
: In a Jev choice or score answer, a number from 0 to 1 that is high when most of the probability is on one option and low when it is spread out. It is not simply the top probability (Chapter 6).


Cost-based threshold
: The probability above which acting is cheaper than not acting, set by what each kind of mistake costs (Chapter 3).

Decision layer
: The part of a system that turns probabilities into actions: typed questions, calibration, thresholds, rules and fail-safes (Chapters 5 and 14).

Decision record
: The logged account of one decision: what was seen, what the model said, what the policy did, which version decided and why (Chapter 13).

Drift
: A change in the world, or in the data, that makes a model's probabilities less accurate than when they were checked (Chapter 10).


ECE (expected calibration error)
: The average gap between what a model said and what happened, across groups of similar predictions (Chapter 2).


Embedding
: A list of numbers that places a word, sentence or item in a space where similar things sit close together (Chapter 4).


Escape option
: The "other", "none" or "not enough information" option that gives cases fitting nowhere somewhere to go (Chapter 7).

Extract, then decide
: A pattern in which an LLM turns messy input into fields and a decision model decides on those fields (Chapter 11).


Fail-safe
: The decided meaning of a failure, such as "if the call fails, send the case to review" (Chapters 10 and 13).



Guardrail gate
: A typed check on trusted facts that runs before an agent's action is allowed to happen (Chapter 11).


Hybrid agent
: An agent in which a decision model answers the small decisions and an LLM only writes (Chapter 11).


Jevons paradox
: When making something more efficient to use makes people use more of it in total, not less (Chapter 14).

JSON mode
: An LLM setting that makes its output valid JSON, though not necessarily correct JSON (Chapter 4).

Label
: The known right answer for an example, used to train or test a model (Chapter 1).

LLM (large language model)
: A model trained to predict the next piece of text, which lets it read and write almost anything (Chapter 4).

LLM-as-judge
: Using an LLM to rate or check an output, often on a numbered scale (Chapter 9).


Logistic regression
: A simple model that works like a credit score: it adds points for each clue and turns the total into a probability (Chapter 2).


Noul
: TypeSafe's name for a yes-or-no question. The answer is the probability of yes (Chapter 7).

Observe, Decide, Act
: The loop an agent runs: read something, choose what to do, do it, repeat (Chapter 5).


Overconfidence
: Probabilities that are more extreme than the evidence justifies. It's common in large models and in overtrained small ones (Chapter 4).


Platt scaling
: A calibration method that fits an S-curve mapping a model's scores to calibrated probabilities (Chapter 2).

Policy
: The rules that turn a probability into an action, usually as thresholds between zones (Chapter 10).


Prompt injection
: Text planted in an input that tries to make a model follow the attacker's instructions (Chapter 5).


RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
: Giving an LLM relevant documents, found by search, before it answers (Chapter 5).


RLCD
: TypeSafe's name for reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions, which it says trains Jev. The details aren't published (Chapter 6).


Router
: A pattern that sends each case to a destination with a choice question, falling back to a person when unsure (Chapter 11).

Score
: A typed question with ordered levels. The answer is a probability for each level and an expected level (Chapter 7).

Shadow mode
: Running a new system or version beside the current one, recording what it would do without letting it act (Chapters 12 and 13).

SIEM (security information and event management)
: The tool that collects a company's logs and raises security alerts. Kestrel's alerts come from one (Chapter 11).


State
: What a decision model reads: the situation, as text or structured fields (Chapter 6).

Structured output
: An LLM answer constrained to a schema, such as JSON with named fields (Chapter 4).

System 1, System 2
: Kahneman's names for fast, automatic thinking and slow, deliberate thinking (Chapter 6).

System One model
: TypeSafe's term for a model that answers typed questions with probabilities in one fast pass, without writing text (Chapter 6).

Temperature (calibration)
: One number that softens or sharpens every probability a model gives, fitted on held-out data (Chapter 2).

Temperature (sampling)
: A setting that makes an LLM's choice of next token more or less random (Chapter 4).

Three-zone policy
: A policy with two thresholds, splitting cases into act, review and escalate (Chapter 10).

Threshold
: A number that splits cases into two groups, like a line on the probability scale: above it you do one thing, below it another (Chapters 1 and 3).

Token
: A piece of text, often part of a word, that an LLM reads and writes one at a time (Chapter 4).

Trace
: The step-by-step record of what an agent observed, decided and did (Chapter 11).

Transformer
: The network design built from attention layers that underlies modern LLMs (Chapter 4).


Triage
: Sorting cases by how likely they are to be real and how urgent they are, so the most important ones are handled first (Preface, Chapter 12).

Typed question
: A question whose answer has a fixed shape: a noul, a choice or a score (Chapter 7).

Vendor-reported
: A claim made by the company selling the product, not independently checked (Chapter 6).
